We implement and evaluate the proposed defense on a sliced 5G testbed integrating Free5GC, UERANSIM, and Containerlab. Experimental results indicate that the XDP-DDM detects and drops malicious nested GTP-U packets at line rate, while the UP-TA and CP-MO asynchronously report and revoke the attacker's network access, respectively. Under a 10,000 packets-per-second cross-slice nested GTP-U flood, the proposed solution preserves the baseline performance of the victim slices while introducing minimal overhead. We also show that the proposed solution has minimal impact on the user's throughput and round-trip time.
items.title: Mitigating Nested GTP Attacks: A Closed-Loop eBPF Defense for 5G and Beyond Networks

items.summary: Backdoor attacks pose a significant security threat to deep neural networks (DNNs) deployed on AI inference engines and hardware accelerators. By embedding hidden triggers during training, these attacks induce malicious behavior while maintaining high accuracy on benign inputs. Multi-trigger backdoor attacks are particularly challenging to detect and mitigate because of the distributed and stealthy nature of their effects. To address this challenge, this paper proposes a training-free Spectral Subspace Filtering framework that detects and suppresses backdoor-induced activations by analyzing latent feature representations. Exploiting the geometric separation between benign and malicious feature distributions, the framework employs Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) to identify the dominant malicious subspace and performs inference-time spectral scrubbing through activation projection. This approach suppresses backdoor effects without model retraining, requiring only a small set of triggered samples collected offline. Experimental evaluation across CNN and transformer architectures, including AlexNet, ResNet18, VGG16, MobileNetV2, and Vision Transformer (ViT), demonstrates that the proposed method reduces the attack success rate (ASR) from 94.2-99.8% to an average of 2.07%, while preserving clean accuracy of up to 98.54% with low inference overhead. The framework also demonstrates robustness across varying poisoning rates and multiple concurrent triggers, highlighting its potential as a lightweight runtime defense for enhancing the security and reliability of AI inference engines against backdoor attacks.
items.title: Lightweight Spectral Subspace Filtering for Trojan-Resilient AI Inference Engines

items.summary: Computing point-to-point shortest paths in large weighted graphs can require classical algorithms to explore a substantial portion of the graph. We ask whether quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) can reduce the work required to return a verified shortest path. For a known set of queries, we select paths that share arcs. For new queries, we select a corridor and test whether any path leaving it could improve the distance found by Dijkstra's algorithm. We also partition the graph into blocks and reuse local paths between their boundaries. We compare path encodings on identical inputs using simulated annealing on classical processors. The comparison of exact block overlays with direct Dijkstra search covered 45 synthetic graphs and the New York road network with 264,346 vertices. The overlay reduced the number of arc inspections in the final search in 97 of 200 graph and block-size combinations. Once endpoint attachment, assembly, and reconstruction were included, every combination took longer per query than direct Dijkstra search. On a separate set of 168 synthetic graphs, tightening the flow penalty increased the fraction of trials returning a verified local optimum within 20,ms from 35.8% to 84.1% under the same annealing schedule and update policy. A cost model for a prepared graph of 16,384 vertices predicts a 1.072x query speedup over a parallel classical overlay if five local problems can be solved accurately in one batch at the assumed service cost. The practical benefit of reduction thus depends on whether savings in the final search cover the cost of obtaining and verifying the local paths.
items.title: Quantum-Annealing-Assisted Search-Space Reduction for Large-Scale Shortest-Path Computation

items.summary: Face verification systems are deployed by selecting a decision threshold that achieves a target false match rate (FMR); performance is then reported as the corresponding false non-match rate (FNMR). In practice, deployed systems operate at FMR $\le 10^{-6}$, but widely used benchmarks can share identities with the models' training corpora. Prior work (Wu et al., 2024) measures the resulting optimistic bias as a small additive change in 10-fold accuracy (up to 1.01 percentage points). We show that the bias is neither small nor constant: it is a multiplicative error that grows as FMR falls. First, we audit train-test overlap with a detector calibrated against a null distribution (rather than a hand-tuned threshold). Relative to WebFace42M, we flag 88.6% of MS1MV3 identities and 14.3% of IJB-C subjects as present, despite WebFace260M's published de-overlap explicitly naming IJB-C. Manual review of 100 flagged IJB-C subjects confirms 69.2%, implying a residual overlap of roughly 9.9%. Second, holding the model fixed, removing only the contaminated identities from the test set increases FNMR by 3.6$\times$ at FMR=$10^{-4}$, 6.3$\times$ at FMR=$10^{-5}$, and 13.9$\times$ at FMR=$10^{-6}$, while a same-size random removal does not. The effect is traced to a shorter impostor tail that lowers the threshold. The magnitude of the shift depends on the training corpus and does not cancel betweent margin between our model and a publicbaseline by half. Third, we give the first direct measurement of the effective number of independent impostor comparisons in IJB-C: only 2.7 million effectively independent comparisons at FMR=$10^{-6}$, which is below all commonly accepted reporting rules. Finallyth a known training corpus, we build areal-face protocol with audited zero overlap that resolves FMR=$10^{-8}$.
items.title: Contamination at the Operating Point: Train-Test Identity Overlap Inflates Low-FMR Face Recognition Accuracy by an Order of Magnitude

items.summary: High-dimensional quantum key distribution tolerates more noise than qubit-based protocols, but the dimension that maximizes the secret key depends on turbulence, background light, device imperfections, and block size, all of which change during an airborne or satellite pass. Finite-size security analyses of high-dimensional protocols fix the dimension in advance, and the dimension-adaptive schemes reported so far have been analyzed only asymptotically. Here, a controller sets the dimension, acceptance thresholds, and key length of each block using only public data from earlier blocks. Each block is therefore a standard fixed-length protocol, and composable finite-key security against coherent attacks follows from sequential composition; an inaccurate channel model reduces the key rate but does not weaken security. The controller estimates turbulence from observed error rates, maximizes the expected key under forecast uncertainty, and recalibrates its model online. We evaluate it on a simulated entanglement-based orbital-angular-momentum link between an aircraft and a ground station, using Kolmogorov phase screens and the Hufnagel--Valley turbulence profile. Accounting for forecast uncertainty increases the key by 31\%--47\% relative to a naive planner. Over night, dawn, daytime, and model-mismatch scenarios, the recalibrated controller retains at least 98.8\% of the key obtained with the best fixed dimension for each scenario, while every fixed dimension drops to 73.5\% or less in at least one scenario. Running the link's measurement statistics on a superconducting quantum processor shows device errors close to a constant offset; with these errors included, the best daytime dimension changes from eight to four, and the controller adjusts accordingly.
items.title: Feed-Forward Dimension Control for High-Dimensional Quantum Key Distribution over Time-Varying Airborne Free-Space Links

items.summary: LLM coding agents authorize shell commands by parsing a command string against a policy and passing the raw string to a system shell, so the gate adjudicates one reading while the shell executes another. We present ParseGap, a differential testing framework that runs each command through an unmodified vendor checker and GNU Bash 5.2 in an isolated container, flagging a violation whenever an approved command produces policy-violating runtime effects. Across eight production coding agents, ParseGap identifies 17 root causes across three divergence boundaries: at the parse, where an upstream tree-sitter-bash defect hides a second command from Mistral Vibe and Gemini CLI; at the utility, where every checker permits read-only binaries whose arguments write files or launch programs (9-47 of 55 cases); and at confinement, where an allow rule in OpenAI Codex CLI disables its read-only OS sandbox. Live trials across two frontier models triggered policy violations in all 16 agent-model pairs (14 under configured restrictions). To eliminate the second reading, we design ShellPlan, which compiles a strict Bash subset once into a typed execution plan, validates utility arguments against positive capability specifications, and dispatches approved plans directly via execve without a shell. Over a formal operational model, we prove single-interpretation dispatch and bound touched programs and files under audited assumptions. ShellPlan admitted 0/4,174 active attacks across six static suites and 0/90 hits in a ten-model agent benchmark (62/90 unguarded) at 1.28 ms median gate latency, preserving 36/36 (100%) frontier standard-dev completion (74/100 overall) and 0/348 external over-allows outside modeled exceptions.
items.title: ParseGap: Testing What Coding Agents Authorize and What Shells Execute

items.summary: Test-time learning (TTL) enables large language models to adapt to unlabeled inputs during deployment. The model updates a lightweight adapter by minimizing the next-token prediction loss on the input it receives. When these updates persist across conversation turns, every user query serves both as the request answered in the current turn and as adaptation data for later turns. By choosing the queries used for adaptation, an attacker can influence parameter updates and weaken safety alignment through ordinary interactions with a TTL chat service. To demonstrate this risk, we introduce Progressive Test-Time Adaptation Poisoning (P-TAP), a query-only multi-turn attack that jailbreaks the model by poisoning its session adapter through the service's own updates. A sequence of escalating adversarial queries shapes the adapter turn by turn; the final harmful request is then answered under the accumulated state without itself being used for adaptation. Across four open-weight instruction-tuned models, enabling updates raises attack success rates on average by 13.00 percentage points under greedy decoding and by 22.25 points under best-of-10 sampling, relative to matched sessions receiving the same queries without updates. Answering adversarial queries but adapting on unrelated text or on benign text about the same topic removes most of this increase. Among existing safeguards, screening incoming queries flags every attack stream before the final request, while a perplexity-based detector of unsafe adaptation flags none of the successful attacks.
items.title: Adaptation or Poisoning? Security Risks of Conversational Test-Time Learning in Large Language Models

items.summary: Robust watermarking for panoramic imagery is impeded by the topological mismatch between spherical signals and planar representations. Conventional methods fail under $SO(3)$ viewing rotations due to non-linear geometric warping and struggle with viewport extraction, which typically necessitates computationally expensive inverse remapping. To address these challenges, we propose RSWP, a watermarking framework grounded in icosahedral group theory. Leveraging the property that the icosahedral group ($\mathcal{I}_{60}$) serves as the largest discrete subgroup of $SO(3)$, we decompose spherical rotations into tractable local planar rotations and combinatorial facet permutations. Accordingly, we introduce a decoupling architecture that embeds watermarks into discrete facets and a theoretically guaranteed Equivariance-to-Invariance decoding paradigm. By employing an equivariant feature extractor followed by a permutation-invariant sorting module, this paradigm rigorously synchronizes rotation-distorted features. Moreover, the dual-extractor design inherently supports direct, blind watermark retrieval from partial 2D renderings without geometric calibration. Extensive experiments demonstrate that RSWP achieves state-of-the-art robustness against continuous $SO(3)$ rotations and viewport transformations while preserving high visual fidelity.
items.title: RSWP: Robust SO(3)-Equivariant Watermarking for Panoramic Images

items.summary: Decoding both uplink and downlink cellular traffic reveals lower-layer protocol behavior, unprotected signaling, and encrypted higher-layer packets beyond what scheduling metadata exposes. In commercial 5G NR networks, however, passive decoding must overcome UE-dedicated configurations hidden in encrypted signaling, unknown identifiers of ongoing connections, and the computational demands of wideband traffic. We present NRSnooper, a passive sniffer that decodes downlink control and bidirectional data traffic in real time, including traffic from already-connected UEs and traffic after encrypted configuration updates. NRSnooper learns reusable physical-layer configurations through an instrumented open-source UE that reproduces commercial UE capabilities. It recovers connection-specific identifiers from ongoing transmissions and selects matching configurations through CRC-validated data decoding. A hybrid CPU-GPU pipeline sustains continuous wideband processing. Evaluations on a controlled testbed and two commercial networks show that, compared with using only configurations from unencrypted signaling, NRSnooper decodes 1.3x and 6.3x as many control messages and 9.0x and 17.7x as many downlink data blocks, respectively. NRSnooper also decodes traffic from an already-connected UE during an ongoing phone call and achieves real-time bidirectional decoding on 100 MHz commercial NR channels.
items.title: NRSnooper: Enabling Real-Time Bidirectional Traffic Decoding in Commercial 5G NR Networks

items.summary: Fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) enables computation directly on encrypted data, but its substantial computational cost hinders adoption in privacy-preserving artificial intelligence (AI) applications. Neural processing units (NPUs) already deployed in AI infrastructure provide a practical platform for FHE acceleration. However, after mapping the number theoretic transform (NTT) to matrix multiplications on Ascend NPUs, modular arithmetic and representation conversion on the Vector backend still incur substantial overhead at stage boundaries. Evaluation-key material of key switching also increases storage and data-transfer costs, and whole-limb task assignment causes tail load imbalance. We present NPUFHE, an end-to-end CKKS execution system optimized for Ascend NPUs. To reduce modular recovery and twiddle costs in NTT, we propose Boundary-Optimized NTT, which eliminates intra-axis modular recovery, compiles intra-axis twiddle factors into matrix constants, and introduces two-level folded modular recovery at axis endpoints. To alleviate evaluation-key storage and transfer pressure, we design Compact Shoup encoding, which halves the key representation through local coefficient recovery. Finally, we propose Cost-Aware Parallel Tiling to mitigate tail load imbalance caused by whole-limb task assignment. It uses a cost model to adaptively partition tail tasks and smooth stepwise latency increases. We integrate the above designs into OpenFHE. On one Ascend 910B4, full-packing CKKS bootstrapping with real evaluation keys takes 0.95 s, encrypted CIFAR-10 ResNet-20 inference with bootstrapping requires 9.87 s per image, and encrypted MNIST inference achieves an amortized latency of 19.81 ms per image. The peak NTT throughput of NPUFHE reaches up to $184.22\times$, $2.04\times$, and $4.46\times$ that of OpenFHE on CPU, TensorFHE, and CROSS, respectively.
items.title: NPUFHE: An Efficient CKKS Execution System for Ascend NPUs

items.summary: Complex packing in CKKS stores two real streams in the real and imaginary lanes of each slot. Direct squaring couples the lanes, while squaring them separately requires two ciphertext-ciphertext multiplications (HMults). DuetFHE is a GPU compiler that uses a phase transformation to square both lanes independently with one HMult. It reuses dual-lane squares in polynomial activations and the modular-reduction stage of CKKS bootstrapping. The compiler further plans ciphertext scales and reuses conjugates to sustain the complex-packed representation across stages. On a single RTX 5090, DuetFHE accelerates four polynomial activations by $1.60$--$1.79\times$ over direct evaluation on two real ciphertexts. For two-image AESPA ResNet-20 inference, it maintains packed execution across convolutions, square activations, and bootstrapping, achieving a $1.97\times$ end-to-end speedup over the fastest tested EasyFHE batched baseline on both the RTX 5090 and RTX PRO 6000.
items.title: DuetFHE: Compiling Dual-Lane Nonlinear Circuits for Complex-Packed CKKS Inference

items.summary: Generative voice cloning threatens voice-based authentication, yet current deepfake detectors rely on power-hungry, high-precision models unsuited to edge hardware. We present SWIFT (Streaming Whiten-Integer Forensic Trust-Engine), a handcrafted detector that works in the high-frequency noise domain where synthesis artifacts concentrate. A first-order integer high-pass residual drives nine families of fixed-point descriptors, among them integer lifting-wavelet cepstral quantiles, Mahalanobis anomaly distances, Poincaré phase-space geometry, and phase jitter, fused by calibrated gradient-boosted trees and a sparse L1-regularised meta-learner. Under leakage-controlled nested cross-validation, with one shared preprocessing chain for real and fake audio, this reference model reaches accuracy of up to 99.86% and an Equal Error Rate (EER) as low as 0.03% across eight benchmarks. Its integer front-end and a fixed-point linear classifier run on the programmable logic of a PYNQ-Z2 (Zynq-7020) board, with a 7.85 microseconds per-frame datapath latency (127.4k frames/s) at 1.734 W and 11.2% LUT utilisation. Integer-only audio deepfake feature extraction is thus feasible at the edge without pretrained neural models or floating-point units.
items.title: SWIFT: A Handcrafted, Arithmetic-Minimal FPGA Engine for Real-Time Audio Deepfake Detection

items.summary: Fully homomorphic encryption enables cloud servers to run neural networks on encrypted inputs. In CKKS, inference requires costly arithmetic on high-degree polynomials. On Ascend neural processing units, preparing operands and reconstructing intermediate results add to this cost, while limited local memory constrains parallel execution. We present AscendFHE, a CKKS backend that coordinates Ascend's matrix engines and vector cores for bootstrapping and encrypted inference. It uses balanced-byte encoding and exact modular reconstruction to reduce vector work and packs intermediate results in the next operator's input format to avoid redundant transfers. Its two-task pipeline reuses shared buffers after their last read to overlap matrix and vector execution within the local memory budget. On Ascend 910B3, AscendFHE achieves a 4.61$\times$ bootstrapping speedup and 1.59$\times$--2.00$\times$ encrypted-inference speedups across ResNet-20, BERT-base, and Llama 3 8B over our Vector-based Ascend port of Cheddar.
items.title: AscendFHE: Efficient Fully Homomorphic Encryption on Ascend NPUs

items.summary: In near-field physical-layer authentication (PLA), the receiver estimates a spatial reference from noisy enrollment pilots. With a fixed residual-energy threshold, even a small reference error can cause the false rejection (FR) probability to approach one as the received energy increases. We derive the distribution of the overlap between the true and enrolled spatial directions and use it to calibrate a test based on the aligned energy and the residual-to-aligned energy ratio. The calibration bounds FR for arbitrary regional gains and all legitimate received energies above a prescribed minimum. For a fixed enrolled reference, we reduce the problem of finding the maximum acceptance probability of a multi-antenna attacker to a one-dimensional search. We also derive a pre-enrollment upper bound that holds when the attacker chooses its precoder after observing the enrolled reference. For a single region and a fixed angular threshold, the enrollment energy sufficient to preserve angular separation grows inversely with the square of the available angular margin. In the numerical study with 128 receive elements at 28 GHz, the FR upper bound was 0.9984, including the enrollment outage allowance. At a regional phase perturbation of 20, four regions provided the best trade-off among the tested partitions: its simulated FR was 0.1442, while its false acceptance (FA) at 9 m was 1.084 under the fixed transmit-energy setting.
items.title: Near-Field Physical-Layer Authentication Under Noisy Enrollment

items.summary: Multimodal web agents automate website interactions but remain vulnerable to visual prompt injection (VPI), where malicious webpage content manipulates their visual processing and induces unintended actions. Although several defenses focus on detecting injected instructions in screenshots, malicious destinations such as phishing URLs embedded in HTML can remain hidden yet accessible through agent interactions. Existing evaluations have also not sufficiently examined adaptive attackers who know the defense mechanisms. To address these limitations, we introduce AdaptiveVPI, the first benchmark for systematically evaluating adaptive VPI threats in web agents. Specifically, we present a dataset of 360 webpage instances spanning 6 distinct hijack strategies across 10 real-world websites, with malicious destinations not visible in screenshots. We design an adaptive attack framework that iteratively refines malicious instructions based on feedback from the defense mechanism being evaluated. We also introduce three metrics to measure the extent of agent hijacking at three different levels. Across 10 defense configurations for computer-use agents and 11 defense configurations for browser-use agents, our adaptive attacks achieve average success rates of 91.87% and 91.99%, respectively. These results reveal a gap between current VPI defenses and realistic threats and highlight the need for defenses designed with adaptive attackers in mind.
items.title: Benchmarking Web Agent Defenses Against Adaptive Visual Prompt Injection

items.summary: Zero-knowledge virtual machines (zkVMs) prove correct execution of programs and underpin systems securing billions of dollars in digital assets. Their security depends on alignment between the instruction set architecture (ISA) that programs target, such as RISC-V, and the constraint system, polynomial equations that check the prover's record of every intermediate value (the witness). Mismatches, or semantic gaps, come in two kinds: underconstraint bugs let a malicious prover forge a proof of an execution the ISA forbids (a soundness violation), and divergence bugs make the zkVM itself deviate from the ISA or crash, so an honest prover cannot prove a legitimate execution (a completeness violation). Both cluster at corner cases such as division by zero that conventional fuzzing almost never reaches, and underconstraint bugs leave program output unchanged. Our key insight is that these corner cases correspond to constraint obligations derived from the ISA specification and the proof system's algebraic structure. We build Beak, a reinforcement-learning fuzzer in which obligations replace three random decisions: they supply inputs that trigger each obligation, reward executions that trigger new combinations of obligations, and direct witness tampering to the step where an obligation is triggered. Beak flags divergence bugs by comparing registers against a reference RISC-V emulator, and underconstraint bugs by checking whether the constraints accept a tampered witness. On six leading production RISC-V zkVMs, Beak detects 25 of 37 known bugs (67.6%) versus 5 (13.5%) for the prior state of the art, and discovers 14 previously unknown bugs, all responsibly disclosed and patched.
items.title: Revealing Semantic Gaps in Zero-Knowledge Virtual Machines via Obligation-Targeted Semantic Fuzzing

items.summary: Fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) enables privacy-preserving large language model inference but remains computationally intensive. Existing multi-GPU FHE inference systems rely on expert-crafted parallelization plans that generalize poorly across hardware platforms and applications. We present \fwName, a framework that automatically compiles CKKS inference programs into efficient multi-GPU executables. Its compiler can split different nodes of the same computation graph at the ciphertext and polynomial level. Guided by a measurement-based performance model, its hardware-aware planner jointly optimizes task partitioning, placement, operand residency, and transfer scheduling. %Critical-path-guided rewrites extract shared computation and restructure homomorphic sums. Its backend then generates optimized GPU kernels and executes plans using CUDA graphs and selective point-to-point transfers. \fwName adapts its plans to diverse hardware configurations and FHE inference algorithms for large-scale models. On a single A100 GPU, \fwName achieves a $24.5\times$ speedup over THOR's reported BERT-Base inference latency. For Cerium's Llama-3-8B workload, \fwName outperforms Cerium's expert-crafted plans by $1.14\times$, $1.16\times$, and $1.24\times$ on 2, 4, and 8 RTX PRO~6000 GPUs, respectively. On A100 GPUs, \fwName achieves $98.0\%$, $91.8\%$, and $79.3\%$ parallel efficiency for the same workload on 2, 4, and 8 GPUs, respectively.
items.title: TurboFHE: An Efficient and Scalable Multi-GPU Framework for Homomorphic LLM Inference

items.summary: Safety alignment is widely used to align large language models (LLMs) to produce helpful and harmless responses. However, an attacker can plant a jailbreak backdoor in an LLM such that adding a universal trigger word or phrase to a harmful prompt elicits attacker-desired responses. Existing jailbreak backdoor attacks induce distinct behaviors on backdoored inputs and safety samples (harmful prompts paired with refusal responses), making the backdoors susceptible to subsequent safety alignment and advanced defenses. In this paper, we propose a persistent jailbreak backdoor attack that reduces the divergence between clean and trigger-conditioned continuations during LLM decoding, making backdoored samples difficult to distinguish from safety samples. We also introduce a deferred-response mechanism that postpones harmful generations, further disguising the backdoor behavior. We evaluate our attack, PJBack, on eight LLMs from five model families, ranging from 7B to 70B parameters. PJBack achieves an average attack success rate of 93.9% and bypasses all seven evaluated defenses while preserving benign utility. In contrast, five existing backdoor attacks either achieve limited attack success or fail to withstand the evaluated defenses.
items.title: Persistent Jailbreak Backdoor Attack

items.summary: Zero-knowledge proofs can show that a neural network produced a given output without revealing the network, but current systems for language models prove integer approximations of the model rather than the floating-point arithmetic that is actually deployed. Proving floating-point matrix multiplication has been regarded as hard, because rounding after every addition makes the result depend on the order of the additions. We avoid this obstacle by proving the correctly rounded product, in which every dot product is computed exactly and rounded once. This result is independent of the hardware and at least as accurate as standard kernels. We give an interactive proof for this relation whose cost is close to that of integer matrix multiplication, with roughly a thousand times fewer committed values than per-operation floating-point circuits need constraints, extend it to every layer of a transformer, and give a privacy construction for the complete argument whose zero knowledge we prove under explicit hypotheses. We implement the system and prove the full forward pass of GPT-2 small, including all twelve blocks and the output over the whole vocabulary, in 19 minutes on two processor cores; verification takes 21 seconds. The verifier rejects all 236 attacks we tested, and the model's outputs agree with high-precision inference at least as closely as standard 16-bit inference does.
items.title: Ziv Meets Sumcheck: Zero-Knowledge Proofs of Floating-Point LLM Inference

items.summary: In rateless transmission the transmitter keeps sending until the legitimate receiver (Bob) can decode. Over a wiretap channel this has a useful side effect: the eavesdropper (Eve) sees only as many symbols as Bob needs, although the transmitter knows neither channel. We study the secrecy of rateless lattice codes in this setting. First, using a public dither and privacy amplification, we prove a finite-length secrecy bound, in total variation distance, for every channel realization, even if Eve knows all codes and seeds and combines all packets. Second, stopping when Bob acknowledges successful decoding, as in hybrid ARQ, costs at most the logarithm of the number of possible feedback outcomes in secret bits. Third, for degraded sessions with state-based stopping and without a pre-shared key or other public discussion, the secret-key rate of a session cannot exceed its accumulated Gaussian secrecy capacity, and adaptive key generation with shaped rateless lattice codes comes within any $ε>0$ of this limit when Eve's channel states are revealed after the session. If only their statistics are known, choosing the key length after the session guarantees a prescribed secrecy-outage probability. Finally, over block Rayleigh fading with a CRC-based acknowledgement and joint belief-propagation decoding, and with Eve $20$~dB weaker on average, the scheme reaches $59$--$69\%$ of the outage-weighted throughput of an ideal infinite-length secure hybrid-ARQ benchmark for Bob SNRs of $8$--$20$~dB.
items.title: Rateless Lattice Codes over Fading Wiretap Channels: Finite-Length Secrecy and the Secret-Key Capacity of Degraded Sessions

items.summary: Confidential GPUs offer near-native on-device compute performance, but transfers between CPU and GPU TEEs through untrusted host memory require bulk CPU encryption and decryption, even for unchanged data. Existing software techniques overlap or parallelize these operations but retain their per-byte CPU cost. Reusing exported ciphertext could avoid this work, but GPU TEE firmware enforces direction-specific encryption keys and fresh per-transfer initialization vectors (IVs), preventing direct reuse. We introduce ciphertext rebinding, a purely software primitive enabling repeated and cross-GPU ciphertext reuse on existing GPU TEEs without hardware changes, while preserving confidentiality, integrity, and freshness. Specifically, ciphertext rebinding exploits the separation between ciphertext-dependent and IV-dependent components in GPU TEE's AES-GCM authentication: a GPU-precomputed summary under the destination key can enable the CPU to update authentication tags without processing the payload. With this modification, GPU's subsequent read on the retained ciphertext can still proceed through the GPU's hardware-fixed copy-engine interfaces, which cannot be modified by software. An additional GPU correction step can then compensate for differences in the keys and IVs to recover the original plaintext. By retaining GPU-exported ciphertext in untrusted host memory, ciphertext rebinding avoids bulk CPU decryption and re-encryption, improving effective bandwidth for GPU-state restoration and sharing. We implement this primitive in HiPerfCC-StateReuse through only driver and library changes, combining batched submissions with pipelined GPU processing and copy-engine transfers. We evaluate transfer efficiency and CPU overhead through microbenchmarks, and application performance through three case studies: model switching, key-value cache offloading, and cross-instance cache sharing.
items.title: HiPerfCC-StateReuse: Ciphertext Reuse for Fast Confidential GPU Data Movement

items.summary: Can we tell whether an LLM is watermarked without knowing its secret key? Published black-box tests suggest that carefully designed prompts can reveal the statistical footprint of a watermark. This paper examines what happens when those tests move from controlled reference implementations to a deployed model whose watermarking parameters are undisclosed. We present an audit of the Red-Green watermark presence test on Claude. Across ten initial configurations, the published test never rejects on a model the provider states is watermarked, despite detecting a local reference at comparable sample sizes. Controlled experiments expose a failure mode: including the prompt in the watermark's repeated-context history suppresses marking exactly where the test measures it. The watermark remains active, but the probe becomes blind. Attempts to repair the probe reveal further confounds. Constructed contexts can trigger native digit-to-word preferences, while comparisons within a single response can measure how the model plans its answer. Tokenization changes which contexts the probe actually controls. These findings show why validation on a surrogate model does not establish validity on the model under investigation. A redesigned probe finds a substantial context-dependent shift on Claude Fable that is absent on two sibling controls. However, the pre-registered decision remains inconclusive because selective refusals violate the protocol, and the effect's watermark origin is unresolved. We show how to design controls, distinguish statistical rejection from evidence of watermarking and interpret a null without treating it as proof of absence. We provide researchers and practitioners working on LLM evaluation, watermarking, and provenance with an audit checklist grounded in concrete successes and failures. Code, prompts, and parsed responses are available for reproducing the analyses.
items.title: Watermark Claims Under Test: Lessons from Auditing a Production LLM

items.summary: Stateful LLM serving engines and agent runtimes reuse execution state and deferred permissions across components and sessions. A cancellation, rollback, or approval is recorded by one component and relied on by another, and recording it does not make the later use valid: a downstream consumer may read state or dispatch an action whose identity, production status, allocation, or target revision has since changed. We call the missing check consumer-time validity and separate two forms. State validity governs what a consumer reads. On vLLM with LMCache, an interrupted KV load leaves unwritten blocks indexed, and a host-only counter rewind desynchronizes the GPU position, so a second tenant generates a schema-valid tool call naming the wrong tenant in 10/10 native-fault runs; the call is recorded and not executed. Authority freshness governs what a consumer executes: on a multi-session approval runtime, an unrevoked deferred grant overwrote a newer revision in one admitted live execution. Output equality cannot test state validity: a fault-free run diverges at token 30 through BF16 batching alone while attended-KV digests match. We therefore specify consumer-bound recovery contracts that, for state recovery, jointly require exclusion, retention, and task completion, and an admissible-witness standard realized as a GPU-free offline trace verifier over scheduler metadata and persisted tool artifacts. On recorded traces the verifier agrees with the reference verdicts in 42/42 frozen GPU-matrix scenarios. An allocation-aware repair satisfies 7/7 triggered vLLM fault predicates on a pinned scheduler-case matrix, where upstream PR 61769 satisfies 2/7, and revision-bound dispatch blocks all 160 deterministic conflicting overwrites in a separate dispatcher cohort. Recovery must be checked where state and authority are consumed, with evidence bound to the consuming request.
items.title: Consumer-Time Validity in Stateful AI Runtimes: Verifying Recovered State and Deferred Authority

items.summary: Practical quantum key distribution (QKD) is secure only while its devices match the assumptions of the security proof, and implementation attacks exploit mismatches while keeping the quantum bit error rate (QBER) low. We formulate attack detection in decoy-state BB84 as a sequential test against the honest-device manifold, the set of receiver statistics an attack-free link can produce under arbitrary channel loss. The resulting monitor, Q-TRACE (Quantum Telemetry Residuals Against Calibrated Expectations), calibrates a physical model of each link on commissioning data, profiles out the transmittance, and combines omnibus residual, physics score and setting-allocation tests with drift-robust references; no attack data are used. The formulation also yields a detectability exponent D* that lower-bounds the delay of any telemetry monitor and vanishes for a Trojan-horse probe with filtered back-reflection. On a count-level twin with model mismatch, over five held-out seeds and at a per-window false-alarm rate of 10^-3, Q-TRACE detects 63.6% of links under known attacks, 28.0% under unseen attack families and 65.3% under composite attacks, versus at most 51.2%, 6.7% and 42.3% for industry monitors, unsupervised and quantum-kernel detectors and a supervised classifier. Its delay attains the bound for strongly detectable attacks. On 33 parallel BB84 links of the IBM Heron processor ibm_marrakesh with physically executed entangling and amplitude-damping eavesdroppers, the measured information-disturbance relations agree with theory; a commissioning reference acquired under different operating conditions triggers alarms in every monitor tested, while a condition-matched reference detects a probe with 0.3% ideal QBER increase on 14 of 14 link-epochs with no false alarm on 66 honest ones.
items.title: Q-TRACE: Physics-based zero-day attack detection for decoy-state quantum key distribution

items.summary: A delegated payment agent can hold valid rights for incompatible revisions of a batch. We study the window in which the selected revision cannot be verified by the execution deadline. For batches that permit every subset of up to q revisions, ActWithin compiles the limit into a shared quota of q successful replacement payments. If approved plans are mutually replayable with the same observable inputs, deadlines, and resources, this quota preserves normal completion without additional approvals and minimizes worst-case wrong-payment principal for arbitrary positive amounts. A dynamic program computes its exact risk and witness. For amount-preserving recipient changes, we derive the exact risk of the tightest single amount cap on the same replacement group, provided mixed payment subsets can settle within the window. A two-phase result isolates the risk to payments due before trusted verification. Against the amount cap, an exploratory setting with 16-64 payments and one quarter of positions revisable yields aggregate reductions of 16.23-16.88% on adapted IBM AMLSim amounts and 10.12-12.52% on an adapted controlled catalog. The 760 funded original controlled paths with constructed single-position revisions yield 2.69%. In one local MetaMask fixture, both policies complete all 37 normal plans and the worst wrong debit falls from 93,962 to 81,056 test wei.
items.title: ActWithin: Bounding Wrong-Payment Risk in Delegated Payment Batches

items.summary: Consensus lets distributed participants agree on a common state, but it makes monetary validity depend on network connectivity and collective acceptance. We explore making validity intrinsic to a digital coin. We propose an \emph{Intrinsic Value Module (IVM)}: trusted hardware that gives a coin locally verifiable authenticity and spendability, analogous to verifying a signature. Under stated hardware and cryptographic assumptions, the IVM abstraction and our offline transfer protocol move monetary uniqueness from a replicated ledger into non-clonable protected state. The protocol prevents forgery, replay, double credit, and double spending by genuine, uncompromised IVMs; communication failures may lock value but cannot duplicate it. We distinguish local transfer atomicity and asset uniqueness, which the protocol establishes, from global state consistency across disconnected devices, which it does not. The IVM does not eliminate trust; it relocates trust to certified hardware, issuer roots, and non-rollback state. We present the architecture, protocol, and security analysis, and discuss open challenges.
items.title: Intrinsic Value Modules: Trusted-Hardware Support for Locally Final Offline Asset Transfer

items.summary: AI agents call external tools through protocols such as the Model Context Protocol (MCP). Some MCP servers return paid advertisements (ads) into the model's context. The model then decides whether these ads and their disclosures reach the user. We trace these ads from their sources to the agent's tool results across public MCP servers and packages. We find the servers through their public traces in ad networks, package registries, certificate logs, hostnames, MCP directories, and GitHub configurations. We then query the ad-serving servers with read-only requests and inspect their ad links. Ads appear on only 0.57% of 101,363 open MCP endpoints and 0.04% of 122,656 local MCP packages. Although 173 ad networks target agents, operators insert the ads themselves on about half of the 226 ad-returning servers. Nearly all ad-serving packages likewise carry the operator's own affiliate identifier. While ads adapt to the topic and intent of the query, their disclosure stays fixed within each tool. Only 9.3% of the ads carry an explicit sponsored label. Most ad links also hide their destinations. Since operators insert most ads themselves and label them inconsistently, we propose a per-item ad annotation in MCP results. Clients can show this annotation to the user independently of the model's answer.
items.title: Ads for Agents: Measuring Ad-Serving MCP Servers

items.summary: In the contemporary artificial intelligence ecosystem, foundation models are increasingly deployed under AI-as-a-Service (AIaaS) schemes characterized by high technical opacity, technological concentration, and limited external auditing capability over governance, training, and internal operational processes. Under these conditions, traditional ethical oversight approaches that focus exclusively on corporate governance or on internal model inspection become insufficient to ensure effective control over AI systems deployed in real-world contexts. This work proposes a pragmatic operational assurance framework inspired by Zero-Trust principles from cybersecurity, which shifts effective auditing efforts toward the application layer, where risk acquires observable, contextualized, and operationally verifiable properties. The proposal articulates two complementary evaluation levels: a black-box evaluation aimed at characterizing general behaviors, vulnerabilities, and risky capabilities of foundation models through conversational scanning, and a grey-box evaluation focused on the operational contextualization of risk within the actual deployment environment of the audited application. The framework incorporates mechanisms to move from general, CVSS-inspired severity metrics toward contextualized operational risk assessments that take into account user profiles, industrial domains, and organizational knowledge. In addition, the proposal strengthens practical auditability through digitally signed explainability reports (signed XAI reports), designed to support verifiable traceability, continuous monitoring, and operational accountability in LLM-based sociotechnical systems.
items.title: Operational Assurance for LLM-Based Systems under Governance Opacity

items.summary: Static malware detectors that represent each sample as a bag of extracted features, such as permissions, API calls, or imported functions, are cheap to deploy and remain state-of-the-art under temporal drift and in selective classification. Yet, attackers can evade them by adding benign-looking content that outweighs malicious evidence. Canonically, detectors encode the presence of a few thousand features, selected during training, as sparse multi-hot vectors over a fixed vocabulary. Features that emerge after training remain invisible. We show that linear models and multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) over this input are sum-pooled set models in disguise. Sum-pooling lets added benign features cancel malicious evidence. Instead, we cast malware detection with set-shaped static features as a multiple-instance learning (MIL) problem. To this end, we propose MalSets, which uses max-pooled Deep Sets models with a monotone head to ensure that any malicious evidence remains undiluted; thus, more is never less. Under MIL, a general text encoder maps any feature string to an embedding, thus eliminating the long-standing out-of-vocabulary problem at test time. Max-pooling retains the malicious evidence regardless of how many benign features an attacker adds. Since max-pooling can only grow when features are added, constraining the head alone makes the malware score monotone under additions, even against a white-box attacker adapted to this architecture. While monotone detectors are never evaded by state-of-the-art black-box or white-box attacks, they often significantly pay for this robustness in clean performance since benign features cannot count as evidence. However, by combining a non-monotone set encoder with max-pooling and a monotone head, MalSets maintains the robustness of prior monotone classifiers while achieving state-of-the-art performance.
items.title: More Is Never Less: Affordable Robustness to Additive Attacks via Monotone Multiple-Instance Learning

items.summary: Large audio-language models (LALMs) have recently been shown to bypass audio CAPTCHAs designed around limitations of automatic speech recognition. To address this threat, we introduce reverse-capability verification, a general CAPTCHA framework that reverses the conventional human-easy, machine-hard relationship with respect to the physical ground truth. It selects challenges in which stable human perceptual limitations cause the human-reference answer to differ from the physical ground truth, while machine analysis tends toward that truth. Because the verifier accepts the human-reference answer, advanced solver capabilities and resulting improved recovery of the physical ground truth may instead strengthen the human-machine separation. We instantiate the framework through psychoacoustics and design two audio CAPTCHAs: HIPI, a classification task, and YINGCHEN, a counting task, together with their conjunctive composition. Across seven LALMs and eight attack strategies, the maximum observed machine acceptance rates are 19%, 17%, and 3% for HIPI, YINGCHEN, and their composition, respectively, compared with 45-100% for nine prior schemes. A multidimensional human usability study yields corresponding human acceptance rates of 78%, 90%, and 76%, while maintaining competitive efficiency and satisfaction. Further analysis demonstrates that advanced LALMs tend toward physical ground truth. These results show that reverse-capability verification substantially reduces machine acceptance while retaining high human acceptance through an approach different from conventional CAPTCHAs.
items.title: When Being Wrong Is Right: Reverse-Capability Audio CAPTCHAs through Psychoacoustic Design

items.summary: The large value $\varepsilon=19.61$, reported as an approximate differential privacy (ADP) parameter for the 2020 U.S. Census, has prompted doubts about the adequacy of Census privacy protection. It was obtained by converting component zero-concentrated differential privacy (zCDP) guarantees to ADP at $δ=10^{-10}$. A single ADP pair can substantially loosen the original upper bound on the power (true positive rate) of a distinguishing test. At significance level $α$, we express the original bound as the smallest pure differential privacy (DP) parameter giving the same power bound. We call this the $α$-operationally equivalent $\varepsilon$. The full curve represents the original bound exactly on $(0,1)$, even when the bound is nonconcave. For maximum-power curves and bounds derived from trade-off functions, we characterize the extrema of operationally equivalent $\varepsilon$ over an interval of significance levels. When finite, they give the parameters of the pure DP bounds that enclose the original power bound on that interval. The mapping preserves the ordering of power bounds at each significance level. For Laplace and Gaussian mechanisms with equal noise variance, conversion to single ADP pairs or Gaussian DP envelopes can reverse this ordering. For the P.L. 94-171 redistricting data, we reproduce the reported $\varepsilon=19.61$ as the sum of rounded component ADP values. The published zCDP guarantee yields operationally equivalent $\varepsilon$ values of approximately 4.25, 2.94, and 3.18 at significance levels of 1%, 5%, and 10%, respectively. Converting the same guarantee to a single ADP pair at $δ=10^{-10}$ gives power bounds near 1 at all three levels. The pure DP scale thus clarifies constraints on distinguishing attacks that are difficult to discern from the reported $\varepsilon=19.61$.
items.title: Reporting Differential Privacy Guarantees via Operationally Equivalent $\varepsilon$: What Does $\varepsilon=19.61$ Mean for the 2020 U.S. Census?

items.summary: AI coding agents now triage issues, review pull requests and pick up tasks inside GitHub repositories, and to do so they read text that anyone with a GitHub account can write. This makes GitHub a prime surface for indirect prompt injection, in which instructions embedded in untrusted content steer a model that later processes it. Prior work has demonstrated such attacks against agents on GitHub in controlled settings, but how often they occur in practice, who deploys them, and for what purpose remain unknown. We present the first large-scale empirical study of AI-directed hidden text on GitHub. We analyzed roughly 145 million issues, pull requests, comments and README files, detected text that GitHub does not render to a human reader but that an agent receives in full, and filtered it with a two-stage LLM classification, a template provenance check and an exhaustive manual review. We identify 2,281 validated findings in issues, pull requests and comments (16 per million items), and AI-directed hidden text in the READMEs of 107 repositories. We find a heterogeneous ecosystem of four uses: attacks on other parties' agents, defensive text that restricts agents, content override that steers what they write, and first-party orchestration, in which projects coordinate their own agents through hidden markers. Attacks are rare (about one in 3.3 million items) but aimed at maintainers' own triage, review and CI agents. Orchestration accounts for two thirds of the findings in issues, pull requests and comments, grew fivefold in four months, and forms a control channel that anyone who can comment can imitate. Replayed offline against five models we tested, the attacks succeed against one small, fast model in 19% of cases, and against none once HTML comments are stripped. We release our detection tool and every finding.
items.title: Who Is Prompt-Injecting Coding Agents? An Empirical Study of Hidden AI-Directed Text on GitHub

items.summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is known to reduce training-data leakage in single-turn interactions, but whether this protection persists over multi-turn conversations is unclear. We introduce CRELT (Conversational RAG Extraction Leakage Trajectory), a reusable framework that tracks, turn by turn, the real contact details from the training data that a RAG system discloses. CRELT separates retrieval, conversation history, and attack strategy through a full-factorial design, uses a retrieval corpus verified to contain none of the target PII, and counts an item as leaked only when it is absent from the model input at the turn it is produced. In our main experiment, this criterion excludes 29-53% of raw matches that were already present in the input. Across GPT-J-6B, Pythia-6.9B, and Pythia-12B, targeting real Enron contact details, retrieval reduces disclosure under both full and cleared history, consistent with prior single-turn results. A length-matched control with random passages reproduces 91-99.5% of this reduction under cleared history and 47-78% under full history, so much of it comes from the added context rather than from what is retrieved. With retrieval enabled, however, retaining full conversation history increases disclosure by a factor of 3.6-4.9, while retaining only one previous turn already restores disclosure to approximately the full-history level. With retrieval, clearing the history reduces disclosure by 72-79%, but does not eliminate it. These results show that single-turn privacy audits can substantially underestimate training-data leakage in conversational RAG systems and that conversation-history policy is a critical dimension of privacy evaluation.
items.title: Beyond Single-Turn Privacy: Training-Data Leakage in Conversational RAG

items.summary: AI coding agents now generate code faster than humans can review it. Security analyses rely on solver answers such as "unsatisfiable" (for example, no attack path exists) or "optimal." Unlike satisfying models, they cannot be checked by looking at them. Formal verification moves trust from code to specifications, but verifiers still place large SAT, SMT, and answer-set solvers, and the translation into solver queries, in their trusted computing base, and these have had soundness bugs. Unlike agent-based pipelines that trust their verifier and solver, our farm trusts no component by default: neither the AI agents, which might make mistakes or game their objectives, nor the solvers. A solver answer counts only if a verified checker accepts its certificate. Every theory, proof, and line of code is generated by AI. For each component, agents first create an Isabelle/HOL theory with a specification, a soundness proof, and a reference checker made by code generation, then a fast Rust implementation, verified with Verus against a specification that mirrors the Isabelle definitions line by line. Specifications are frozen after independent review and cannot be changed by the implementing agents. A trust manifest lists what is still trusted. We built trust chains for SAT (verified LRAT checking); SMT, with certificates from an extended z3 and verified bit-blasting for bit-vectors and floating point; answer-set programming, with native certificates from clingo, including weight rules and optimality; and, closing the loop, Verus's final verification-condition step, by translation validation. All 3,726 SMT queries from 20 crates are certified and validated, and 15,662 answer-set proofs are accepted by both the Isabelle and the Verus checker. We found soundness defects in three proof checkers, including drat-trim, and in five solvers, including clasp and z3, which report wrong unsatisfiability.
items.title: Zero-Trust Formal Methods: AI Agents Build Verified Checkers for Untrusted Solvers

items.summary: Hierarchical key-value (KV) caching reduces repeated prefill computation in large language model serving by retaining reusable state beyond GPU memory. Under GPU confidential computing (CC), however, protected transfers can erase this benefit. We show that bulk KV copies hold driver locks during prolonged CPU-side processing, stalling independent serving operations despite separate threads and streams. Our characterization on Hopper and Blackwell GPUs shows how lock scope, copy granularity, and allocation ownership affect foreground progress and transfer parallelism. Guided by these findings, we present HiPerfCC-KVCache, which manages resource lifetimes, prioritizes ready token readback between bounded backup submissions, and parallelizes KV restores through auxiliary contexts with shared GPU staging. Implemented in SGLang, HiPerfCC-KVCache uses existing protected transfer interfaces without hardware or driver changes. Across three models and three workloads on H200, HiPerfCC-KVCache achieves a geometric-mean output-token throughput speedup of $1.74\times$ (up to $2.72\times$) over the staged KV-transfer HiCache-Workers baseline at the highest tested loads. Mean time to first token decreases by 36% on average and up to 59%. The benefits generalize to RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell, with a geometric-mean throughput speedup of $1.28\times$ (up to $2.20\times$) over the same baseline. A capacity analysis further models and explains variation in gains and remaining gaps to CC-off serving.
items.title: HiPerfCC-KVCache: Accelerating Confidential LLM Serving with Hierarchical KV Caching

items.summary: QR-UOV is a Quotient Ring Unbalanced Oil and Vinegar (UOV) multivariate quadratic (MQ) signature scheme that has progressed to round-3 of the post-quantum cryptography (PQC) additional signatures call by the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST). Until now, for architectural efficiency and performance trade-offs, QR-UOV has been evaluated only on software platforms and has never been considered on hardware, such as field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs). To address this, we are the first to provide a complete QR-UOV hardware implementation through a flexible and unified QUISA coprocessor design, which supports instruction-driven execution for key generation, signing, and verification across all three NIST security levels (SL-I, SL-III, SL-V). The proposed architecture features extensive throughput optimizations by parallelizing key QR-UOV module operations, such as the pseudorandom byte generator, hashing, and rejection sampling. To minimize hardware resources, we propose a modular arithmetic unit with finite-field reduction based on the shift-add folding method. The design introduces a linear system solver for QUISA based on LU decomposition with partial pivoting and a sample solution module, operating over the prime field Fq (q = 127). We comprehensively evaluate QUISA on an Artix-7 FPGA at 80 MHz up to the post-place-and-route stage, utilizing 11,144 slices and 35,248 look-up tables. For higher SL-V security levels, it completes key generation, signing, and verification in 30.4M, 3.8M, and 2.8M clock cycles, respectively.
items.title: QUISA: A Compact, Flexible and Unified Instruction-Set Coprocessor for QR-UOV Signature

items.summary: Tor end-to-end correlation attacks can link a client to its destination by matching traffic observed at both ends of a Tor circuit. However, their practical threat remains unclear for two reasons: existing correlation methods rely on O(N^2) pairwise processing, and prior works do not reflect the flow counts and base rates seen by realistic adversaries. We present InstantCoFFEA, which replaces exhaustive pairwise search with approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) retrieval using CAGRA and introduces ranked voting. At N = 200k, InstantCoFFEA is 14.56x faster than DeepCoFFEA and improves PR-AUC from 0.94 to 0.96. We also use TorPS to estimate the flow counts and matching-pair base rates observed by relay-level and network-level adversaries. Our simulations show that realistic attacks involve substantially more candidate flows and much lower base rates than those used in prior evaluations. Under a low-base-rate setting, PR-AUC drops for all methods, but InstantCoFFEA achieves 0.53 compared with 0.42 for DeepCoFFEA. These results show that evaluating correlation attacks requires considering both computational scale and the sparsity of true matching pairs.
items.title: InstantCoFFEA: Fast and accurate Tor flow correlation at realistic scale

items.summary: In 2001 we published a paper on an Anti OS Detection (AoD) system: a modified FreeBSD 4.3 kernel that makes a host answer the probes of an OS fingerprinting tool as if it ran another operating system. This report revisits that work on FreeBSD 15.1. We do not claim a new method. We report three things. First, the same goal is now reachable from a loadable module of about 800 lines that uses the packet filter hook interface and sets one kernel variable, without changing the kernel source. Second, the module covers both active and passive fingerprinting: Nmap 7.98 reports an exact match for Linux and for Windows 10/11, and p0f 3 reports the same systems from the connections the host opens. Third, an exact match in Nmap was not enough: a passive tool, plain FIN scans and a comparison with real hosts each exposed a mismatch that the previous step could not see. A real Windows 11 host and the final Windows personality get the same verdict from Nmap and the same signatures from p0f and JA4T; a real Linux 7.0 host is not an exact match in Nmap at all, while the personality built from Nmap's database is. We describe those mismatches, how we removed them, what the module costs, and what it still cannot hide.
items.title: Anti OS Fingerprinting, Revisited: A Loadable Kernel Module for FreeBSD and What Twenty-Five Years Changed

items.summary: Stochastic computing (SC) encodes numerical values as probabilistic bit-streams and enables arithmetic operations using simple logic gates, offering a promising paradigm for low- cost, fault-tolerant, and highly parallel computation. However, the accuracy and efficiency of SC systems depend on the quality of the stochastic number generator (SNG). Conventional SNGs rely on pseudo-random or quasi-random generators, whose deterministic nature introduces periodicity, correlation, and bias, limiting achievable accuracy and robustness. This paper proposes a low- cost arbiter physical unclonable function (APUF)-based SNG that operates in near-metastable delay conditions to generate true- random stochastic bit-streams with controllable output probabilities. By selecting input challenges that drive the path delay difference toward a target value, the resulting output probability is governed by intrinsic device noise, eliminating the need for conventional random-number generators and comparator-based SNGs. The proposed design inherits the low hardware overhead and statistical independence properties of the APUF structure. A probabilistic model and a challenge selection method are developed to characterize and control the stochastic behavior. An 8-stage APUF-SNG matches the 1% mean absolute error of state- of-the-art true-random SNGs at 1024-bit streams and occupies 116μm^2 in 45nm, 2.5x and 7x smaller than the TRNG-based and Sobol-based generator designs, respectively.
items.title: APUF-SNG: A Low-Cost Arbiter-PUF Stochastic Number Generator with Tunable Output Probability

items.summary: Developing deep learning models requires substantial computational and data resources, making them core intellectual assets for enterprises. As Deep Learning as a Service (DLaaS) increasingly extends to edge computing environments, models deployed on third-party devices face growing threats from reverse engineering. Existing model protection methods often depend on specialized hardware or incur substantial computational overhead, while lacking effective mechanisms for controlling model usage. There is therefore a need for lightweight solutions that combine model protection with controllable authorization. To address this challenge, we propose KeyObf, a model obfuscation and controllable authorization scheme for DLaaS. KeyObf efficiently protects model parameters and architecture through model obfuscation while binding parameter recovery to user keys, ensuring that only authorized users can perform inference correctly. By integrating a key-based mechanism into the obfuscation framework, KeyObf unifies model protection and controllable authorization. Experimental results demonstrate that KeyObf preserves the inference accuracy of authorized users, rejects inference requests when credential authentication fails, and increases the difficulty of recovering model information under the evaluated reverse-engineering conditions. These results demonstrate the feasibility of a lightweight approach to model protection and controllable authorization in third-party deployment scenarios.
items.title: A Model Obfuscation and Controllable Authorization Scheme for Deep Learning as a Service

items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to detect vulnerabilities, and their benchmark scores are often read as evidence that they understand the vulnerabilities they report. We test this reading against program execution. For 515 C and C++ functions from BigVul and PrimeVul whose vulnerability we reproduce with a proof of concept, we identify the line at which the fault occurs and the statements on which the faulting run depended. These facts ground a ladder of five tests, from telling a vulnerable function from its fixed version, through locating the fault and reacting to its removal, to judging execution-confirmed edits and predicting the outcome of a concrete run. Each test is paired with a baseline that needs no understanding, such as a rule that picks lines with risky calls, and we repeat the study on 195 vulnerabilities published after the training cutoffs of the models. Four findings emerge. First, telling a vulnerable function from its fixed version is hard. The open-weight models separate no more pairs than chance, although five of them show a weak sensitivity to the fix, and the commercial models still label many screened fixed versions vulnerable. Second, the commercial models locate the fault beyond a keyword rule, while removing that evidence changes the verdicts of the strongest model only on the newer vulnerabilities. Third, given the program input, the commercial models predict whether a run faults better than a rule that looks for added checks, and the prediction follows the input. Fourth, on the newer vulnerabilities this advantage disappears and the lead of the strongest model narrows, while localization persists. We release the framework, the per-function evidence, and an execution-confirmed counterfactual benchmark.
items.title: Right Verdict, Right Reason? An Execution-Grounded Study of Whether LLM Vulnerability Detectors Understand Vulnerabilities

items.summary: Witness encryption encrypts a message to an NP statement so that whoever holds a witness can decrypt. Over a decade after its introduction, known constructions for general NP statements are far from practical or rest on heuristic or broken assumptions. We propose Praxis, a practical scheme for NP, and prove it extractable in the bilinear generic group and random oracle models under Module-SIS. Our instantiation encrypts to a Groth16 verifier on BN254, set up honestly, which serves every NP relation at the same cost: at $100$-bit security, its ciphertext is $7.88$ GiB, encryption takes $2^{34.2}$ base-field multiplications, and decryption with a Groth16 proof $2^{33.0}$ on average. We give Lean 4 proofs of correctness and extraction at this instantiation's parameters. Praxis starts from the rank-gap template of the recent feasibility result [Hair and Sahai, arXiv 2026]. Where they raise the gap to keep decryption polynomial, we fix it, so decryption ends with a search that is exponential but concretely fast: $O(2^{λ/4} N^{1/4})$ expected operations for a statement in $N$ Boolean unknowns at $λ$-bit security. A quadratic arithmetic program makes our hidden matrix low rank, so where their ciphertext encodes a basis of a matrix space, ours holds factors of width two, which a pairing multiplies. Weights and identities from an extension field tie copies of this matrix, so an adversary telling encryptions apart yields a witness or a Module-SIS solution. For the same Groth16 statement and $100$-bit security level, Praxis reduces the ciphertext size and the cost of encryption of either of their constructions by over ten orders of magnitude, and that of decryption by over six.
items.title: Praxis: Practical Witness Encryption for NP

items.summary: Open-weight language models are vulnerable to trigger-conditioned behaviors introduced through sparse post-training weight modifications, creating supply-chain risks beyond conventional provenance checks. We present Neural Sentinel, a cross-architecture study of gradient-guided backdoor insertion and model forensics spanning 18 checkpoints across 14 architecture families (124M-31.3B parameters), including state-space and recurrent models. On Phi-2, modifying approximately 0.0002% of parameters induced an exact short-marker output after 300 steps (332 seconds), with mean next-token KL divergence of $1.5 \times 10^{-5}$ and 100% top-1 agreement over evaluated positions of eight fixed reference prompts. Separate experiments produced structured tool-call-formatted outputs without establishing downstream execution. We identify three procedure-dependent response regimes -- Gradient-Permeable, Scale-Threshold, and Gradient-Fragmented -- and evaluate PPO-based weight-space exploration, which showed no statistically significant advantage over random search. For defense, Neural Sentinel combines weight-difference analysis, trigger discovery, activation probing, and contextual output inspection. In a 22-artifact development cohort, its reference-optional scanner classified 4/5 backdoored artifacts as BACKDOORED; the remaining positive and all 17 clean artifacts were SUSPICIOUS. These findings establish the feasibility of sparse conditional-output insertion and evidence-producing forensic triage, while identifying limitations in behavioral-drift assessment and clean-model admission.
items.title: Weight-Space Backdoors in Open-Weight LLMs: Cross-Architecture Attacks and Blind Model Forensics

items.summary: Distributed backdoor attacks split a trigger among several federated learning clients, so that the backdoor appears only in the aggregated model. Since DBA, a line of work has reported that such attacks are stronger, more persistent, and stealthier than a single attacker with the full trigger. We systematize this literature and test this belief. We code nineteen primary studies and fifteen papers that evaluate against DBA. The reported advantage is rarely measured against a complete trigger delivered by the same attackers, and none of the fifteen evaluations tests whether individual pieces remain effective. We then run 875 paired federated runs that separate adding attackers from splitting the trigger. In our image experiments, adding attackers raised attack success in every seed of all 30 cells where we measured it, by 7.5 to 83.4 percentage points on average. Splitting the trigger among the same attackers had a smaller effect, and its sign depended on the piece layout, the allocation, and the attackers' local training. With DBA's compact layout, splitting lowered attack success on CIFAR-10. A larger penalty on small CNNs vanished once the attackers trained longer, and an FCBA-style allocation gained a few points. Widely separated pieces helped on CIFAR-10, its grayscale version, and GTSRB. No model required all pieces. Neural Cleanse suppressed single pieces together with the full trigger, but split backdoors with separated pieces survived it better than complete ones. We derive reporting requirements for attack and defense evaluations.
items.title: SoK: Splitting the Trigger or Adding Attackers? Disentangling Distributed Backdoor Attacks in Federated Learning

items.summary: We study stochastic convex optimization with heavy-tailed stochastic gradients under $(\varepsilon, δ)$-user-level differential privacy, which protects each user's entire collection of samples. Instead of assuming a uniformly bounded Lipschitz constant, we only assume bounds on the second- and $k$-th moments of the random sample Lipschitz parameters. This allows for unbounded, heavy-tailed stochastic gradient distributions and can lead to sharper excess risk bounds. We characterize the minimax optimal excess population risk up to logarithmic factors. Our algorithm achieves the optimal rate with only $\widetilde{O}(1/\varepsilon)$ users. As a byproduct of our algorithmic developments, we obtain tight bounds for user-level private mean estimation under norm-moment assumptions, improving over the guarantees of Esfandiari et al. (2022) and Zhao et al. (2024). Finally, for mean estimation under the directional-moment assumption of Agarwal et al. (2025), we close their remaining approximate-DP gap by removing the additional $d/\varepsilon$ user requirement and attaining the optimal sample complexity up to logarithmic factors.
items.title: Optimal User-Level Private Stochastic Convex Optimization and Mean Estimation with Heavy Tails

items.summary: Agentic coding tools turn a specification into a running web application, so their defaults for authentication, sessions, input validation, and dependencies become its security posture. This study asks whether appending a fixed block of OWASP-aligned security requirements to the prompt changes what such tools produce, by how much, and with what side effects. Each of 100 frozen specifications was realized four times: two agentic tools (Claude Code, Codex CLI) crossed with two prompts sharing a byte-identical functional core, without (A) and with (B) the security block. A fixed static and dynamic pipeline scanned the 400 applications, yielding 6,721 triaged findings, analyzed with count and logistic mixed models and with a dependency diff. The block cut findings per application by a third (incidence-rate ratio 0.65, 95% CI 0.60-0.71), equally through both tools, and roughly doubled the declared dependency surface, so variant-B applications carried more high-severity dependency advisories. Adjusted for that surface the advisory rate did not rise (flat per application, 18% lower in aggregate), while high-severity findings in first-party source fell by nearly half. Security-focused prompting is therefore an inexpensive and portable improvement, but it enlarges the dependency surface that has to be audited against it, an effect of library selection rather than of the security requirements themselves.
items.title: The Effect of Security-Focused Prompts on Reported Findings: A Controlled Experiment on 400 AI-Generated Web Applications

items.summary: Tabular foundation models (TFMs) predict the label of a query row conditioned on a context of labelled rows, without training on them. Drawn from operational data, the context becomes an attack surface. We study targeted in-context poisoning in its simplest form: an attacker with write access to the context's source places exact copies of a target row there with the wrong label. On 30 OpenML datasets for binary classification, one such poison row flips on average 53% (TabICL) and 65% (TabPFN) of the predictions correct without attack, and three poison rows flip almost all. The same copy with the true label flips almost none, and performance on the remaining rows hardly changes. Predictions flip by two routes: in TabICL, the target row's embedding rotates towards the mean of the wrong class; in TabPFN, the poison row pulls genuine rows of the wrong class along. The TFMs thus infer soundly, but from forged evidence. Predictions of trained models flip as well: almost always for a random forest, for CatBoost as often as for the TFMs, hardly for a logistic regression. New with TFMs is not the kind of vulnerability but the timing: the data take effect at the moment of prediction, not through training, and a poison row in a live context can be deleted afterwards. Three established requirements must therefore cover the context: access control for its source, traceability per prediction, which can also deter, and validation at prediction time. A detection mechanism shows how such validation can work.
items.title: Targeted In-Context Poisoning of Tabular Foundation Models: An Empirical Study

items.summary: Electroencephalography (EEG) signals contain sensitive, subject-specific information, making models trained on them potential targets for membership inference attacks (MIAs). Although MIAs have been studied extensively in other domains, their applications to EEG models are relatively scarce, and the factors driving the vulnerability of EEG models to MIAs are not adequately understood. In this paper, we present a systematic empirical analysis of MIAs on EEG models using three datasets, seven model architectures, four attack methods, and two metrics. Results show that poor model generalization (large train-test loss and accuracy gap) is the strongest indicator of MIA vulnerability. Longer training and larger models also increase vulnerability. Moreover, no particular scalp region, frequency band, inter-channel correlation pattern, or temporal versus spectral representation of EEG data consistently explains MIA vulnerability across datasets. Finally, subject identification and leave-one-subject-out experiments indicate that models relying more heavily on subject-specific representations are more vulnerable to MIAs. Overall, our findings identify the key drivers of membership leakage in EEG models and can provide guidance for developing MIA-resilient EEG systems.
items.title: Understanding Membership Inference Attacks on EEG Models

items.summary: Latent dynamic world models have proven to be highly versatile tools for embodied artificial intelligence systems, enabling online action planning, safe policy evaluation, and scalable policy learning. However, this versatility makes world models a vulnerable and centralized point of failure as a compromised model can impact planning, evaluation, and training at once. Therefore it is critical that the security and robustness properties of world models are properly understood before they are universally deployed in embodied AI systems. In this work we take a unifying approach towards this understanding, developing two novel attacks against world models, named state hallucination and dynamic shift attacks, aimed directly at impacting downstream systems, and proposing a new theoretical lens through which to study the robustness of latent dynamic world models. Through our analysis we identify robust latent space encoders as the key component of robust world models. We empirically validate this finding on four separate latent dynamic world model families, studying Dino World Model, Le World Model, r2Dreamer, and Cosmos 3, demonstrating significant improvements in robustness through adversarial encoder model training.
items.title: Toward Adversarially Robust World Models
