items.summary: Machine learning (ML) property attestation lets a model provider demonstrate properties of their models and datasets to verifiers, and trusted execution environments (TEEs) have emerged as its most practical mechanism. However, existing TEE-based systems attest only a static snapshot of the TEE's initial configuration, leaving run-time behavior unauditable. Proof of execution (PoX) architectures close this gap by requiring the prover's root of trust to also demonstrate that (1) the attested operation actually executed and (2) the claimed outputs were affected only by that operation. Existing PoX designs, though, target microcontrollers and rely on hardware features unavailable in server-grade TEEs, so they cannot be applied directly to ML workloads. We present EVOLVE, a software-based PoX framework for server-grade TEEs. EVOLVE mediates an operation's writes and control flow to track whether a requested ML operation executes without violation. It binds the execution status to measurements of the operation's inputs and outputs, enabling verifiers to assess run-time behavior through ML property attestation. We implement EVOLVE on Intel TDX as a Rust module within its virtual firmware, with policy checks built on primitives formally verified in F*. Our evaluation shows that EVOLVE is versatile across diverse ML applications on unmodified hardware, provides formal guarantees for its policy checks. EVOLVE incurs per-request run-time overhead on average ranging from 1.07$\times$ (for decision trees) to 2.13$\times$ (for multi-layer perceptrons).
items.title: Enabling Verifiable Output Lineage for Virtualized ML Workload Execution

items.summary: This paper investigates the cyber-economic impact and pre-clearing detectability of false data injection attacks (FDIAs) in peer-to-peer (P2P) energy trading among interconnected microgrids. In the proposed cyber-economic framework, load and photovoltaic profiles drive a sequential 15-minute market with deterministic double-sided proportional (pro-rata) allocation and supply-to-demand-ratio (SDR) pricing, while true physical injections are separated from communicated market quantities. The framework is evaluated through a multi-microgrid case study over 69,904 market-aligned states, for which all AC power-flow solutions converged and voltages remained within 0.98999-1.04369 per unit. Healthy local exchange reached 1,159.66 MWh and generated USD 92,772.62 of community benefit. Bias, scaling, and ramp attacks modify only one microgrid's communicated quantity, altering the settlement price, P2P allocation, scheduled residual-grid exchange, participant financial outcomes, and benefit fairness, while true feeder injections remain unchanged. Role-specific random forest, statistical threshold, and score-fusion detectors are compared using only information available before clearing. Pooled sample-level detection rates range from 7.82% to 12.14%, with false-alarm rates from 4.69% to 7.70% and role dependence. In the investigated case study, measurable downstream economic distortion and low pre-clearing detectability coexist under bounded quantity manipulation.
items.title: Quantity-Level FDIA in SDR-Based P2P Energy Trading: Cyber-Economic Impact and Pre-Clearing Detection

items.summary: Abliteration is a widely used white-box attack against the safety alignment of large language models (LLMs). It elicits harmful behavior by estimating a refusal direction in the model's activation space and projecting that direction out of the residual-stream write-out matrices. We propose INSEP, a defense that fine-tunes the model to reduce the separability of harmful and benign activations along the refusal direction. Abliteration estimates this direction as a difference in class means and projects it out. Reducing separability weakens the signal the attack relies on. An adversarial eigendecomposition selects the most separable prompt subsets. A low-rank adapter reduces their separation along that direction. Behavioral losses preserve the base model's refusal and the quality of its benign responses during training. We benchmark INSEP against six published defenses under five attacks, across eight LLMs from 1B to 14B parameters and several model families. Beyond response harm, we measure coherence, directness, over-refusal, and MMLU, to distinguish robust refusal from low harm produced by evasive or degraded responses. INSEP ranks first on the mean composite score across all eight base models while retaining utility, in the largest abliteration-defense evaluation reported to date.
items.title: INSEP: Refusal-Direction Inseparability as a Defense Against Abliteration

items.summary: Conventional Machine Learning (ML)-based Intrusion Detection Systems (IDSs) require manual design, optimize only detection performance, and neglect inference latency and model size, which are critical for resource-constrained Internet of Things (IoT) and Electric Vehicle Charging System (EVCS) deployments. Automated ML (AutoML) reduces manual effort but explores broad search spaces inefficiently. Meanwhile, Multi-Objective Optimization (MOO) methods lack guided search initialization, leading to long search times. This paper proposes a Large Language Model-Assisted Multi-Objective Automated ML (LLM-MOO-AutoML) framework for efficient intrusion detection. A local Llama 3.1 8B model analyzes a compact dataset profile and generates a bounded, validated policy for automated data balancing (AutoDP) and feature engineering (AutoFE). This policy narrows the search space for Non-dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm III (NSGA-III), which jointly optimizes the LightGBM feature-selection threshold and key hyperparameters across three objectives: maximizing weighted F1-score, minimizing 99th-percentile (P99) inference latency ratio, and minimizing model size ratio. Experiments on CICIDS2017, IoTID20, and CICEVSE2024 demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves the highest weighted F1-scores on CICIDS2017 (99.788%), IoTID20 (99.778%), and CICEVSE2024 (99.989%), with feature sets reduced to as few as 10 features, P99 latency as low as 0.00038 ms, and model size as small as 0.1073 MB. The LLM-guided configuration reduced NSGA-III search time relative to unconstrained multi-objective search on all datasets at the largest trial budget and in most comparisons at smaller budgets, indicating that dataset-aware search-space reduction supports efficient, deployment-aware intrusion detection.
items.title: An LLM-Assisted Multi-Objective AutoML Framework for Efficient Network Intrusion Detection
